lessons.title: Commission-approved forms and the practice-of-law line
lessons.body:
## Why Colorado brokers fill in forms at all

Drafting a contract for someone else is normally the practice of law. Colorado brokers are allowed to complete contracts anyway because of two things working together:

- **The Conway-Bogue decision (1957).** In [[Conway-Bogue]], the Colorado Supreme Court agreed that filling in deeds, notes, deeds of trust and similar documents *is* the practice of law, but it refused to stop brokers from doing it as part of their regular business. The conditions it described still shape the rules: brokers fill in blanks on standard printed forms, only in transactions where they are acting as the broker, and they take no fee for the paperwork beyond their ordinary commission.
- **The license law, C.R.S. 12-10-403(4).** A broker working as a single agent or as a transaction-broker may complete "standard forms" for a real estate transaction.

### What brokers may not do

- Prepare documents for transactions they are not brokering (as a favor or a side business).
- Charge a separate document-preparation fee.
- Draft original legal language or act as a party's lawyer.
- Rely on their own judgment when legal complications arise. That is the point to send the party to an attorney.

> **Exam tip:** "The broker charged $150 to prepare the deed" or "the broker drafted a custom clause because the parties couldn't afford a lawyer" points to unauthorized practice of law.

## The eight kinds of standard forms

The statute lists the forms a broker may complete:

| Category | Broker's limits |
|---|---|
| [[Commission-approved form]] | Must be used whenever one exists and is appropriate |
| Form drafted by a Colorado attorney for the broker or firm (names of the attorney and broker/firm on the form) | Only when no appropriate Commission-approved form exists |
| Form provided by a party the broker works with | Insert transaction-specific information only. Keep written confirmation of who supplied the form |
| Form required by a government agency or regulated lender | Insert transaction-specific information only |
| Form approved by the Colorado Bar Association | Only when no appropriate Commission-approved form exists, and within the Bar's guidelines |
| Disclosure-only form | Gives information. Can't create or waive legal rights |
| Title company closing form | When the title company is doing the closing |
| Letter of intent | Must say on its face that it is nonbinding |

**The rule to remember:** if a Commission-approved form exists and fits the transaction, the broker must use it. In every transaction, the broker must tell the parties that the forms have important legal consequences and that they should consult legal counsel before signing.

### Builder, bank and other principal-supplied contracts

Builders, banks selling REO property and some institutional sellers often insist on their own contract. A broker representing the consumer may work with that contract, but the broker should advise the client in writing to get legal advice before signing. The broker only inserts transaction-specific information. The broker doesn't rewrite the principal's form.

### When the broker is a party

A broker buying or selling for their own account is acting as a principal. Under the Commission's position, the broker still uses a Commission-approved form when one exists and must disclose in writing that they are licensed. The forms page also allows a broker who is a party to have their own attorney prepare a form, as long as it conspicuously states that it is **not** a Commission-approved form.

## Changing a form: what's allowed

Commission rules on using forms boil down to these points:

- You may add firm identification and initial lines, and make blanks longer or shorter.
- Printed text is deleted only because of negotiation or a party's instruction. It is struck through so it can still be read. It is never silently erased.
- Inserted language must be in a font that stands out from the printed text.
- If a section doesn't apply, its caption stays and the text is marked as omitted or not applicable.
- The broker must explain every change and addendum to the principal.

### Additional Provisions

The [[Additional Provisions]] section is where negotiated, deal-specific terms go. The form itself notes that this language is not Commission-approved. The guardrails:

- The broker writes down what the parties actually agreed. It must come from negotiation or the parties' instructions.
- Simple factual statements are fine ("Seller to leave the garage refrigerator").
- Legal drafting is not fine. If a clause needs a lawyer, an attorney drafts it, and the broker must understand it before using it. Commission rules also make the broker keep a copy of an attorney-drafted clause, with the attorney's name, for **4 years** from its last use and provide it to the Commission on request.
- A broker who is not a party may not add an exculpatory clause that protects the broker.

> **Exam tip:** Additional Provisions are for recording facts the parties agreed to. They are not a place for the broker to write legal language or to protect the broker.

## Matching the form to the property

All current sales contracts carry a January 1, 2026 mandatory-use date.

| Situation | Contract |
|---|---|
| Single-family home, condo or townhome | **Residential** (CBS1) |
| Income-producing residential: 1–4 units or larger | **Income-Residential** (CBS2): leases, rent roll, tenant estoppels, security deposits |
| Office, retail, industrial, mixed use | **Commercial** (CBS3): Phase I environmental, ADA review, estoppels. A Residential Addendum is attached if there are residences |
| Vacant or rural land | **Land** (CBS4): growing crops, water rights, mineral rights. A Residential Addendum is attached if there are residences |
| Homeowner in foreclosure selling to an investor | **Residential (Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act)** contract |
| Manufactured home on a leased lot | **Manufactured Home Contract to Buy and Sell (Lot Lease Only)** |

The Commission's current list doesn't include a separate farm and ranch contract. If a deal doesn't fit any current form, talk to your managing broker or an attorney before improvising.

There are **no Commission-approved leases or property management agreements.**

## Form versions change

The Commission revises the forms periodically. Each revision has an adoption date and a mandatory-use date, which is often January 1. The Division posts upcoming versions ahead of time "for informational purposes." Using an outdated version after its replacement becomes mandatory violates the requirement to use the Commission-approved form. Whatever transaction software you use, make sure it has the current version.

This course teaches the versions mandatory on January 1, 2026. In August 2026 the Commission adopted another round of revisions, mandatory **January 1, 2027**. The Division lists substantive changes to the listing contracts (Exclusive Right to Sell, Exclusive Right to Buy and the lease/tenant listings), the Inspection Resolution, the Appraised Value Objection Notice, the title objection notice (renamed **Title, Survey and Due Diligence-Related Objection Notice**), both Short Sale Addenda, the Source of Water Addendum, the lead-based paint forms, the notes and deeds of trust, the brokerage disclosures and the Foreclosure Protection Act notices. The Counterproposal, Agreement to Amend/Extend, Notice to Terminate and Earnest Money Release got header-only changes. The 2026 sales contracts themselves aren't on the 2027 list. **Check the current form** on the Division's website before you rely on any section-level detail in these lessons.

> **Exam tip:** "Which form?" questions usually turn on the property's use, not its zoning or price. Use Income-Residential for a fourplex investment, Commercial for a strip center, and Land for raw acreage.

lessons.title: The residential contract, part 1: price, deadlines, financing and appraisal
lessons.body:
## The structure of CBS1

The Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential) is about 20 pages and follows a fixed order. Learn what each section does, not its paragraph numbers:

1. Parties and property, including inclusions, exclusions and water rights
2. The **Dates, Deadlines and Applicability** table
3. Purchase price and terms, including [[earnest money]]
4. Financing conditions, then appraisal
5. Owners' association documents
6. Title (record and off-record), then the new ILC or survey
7. Seller's disclosures, inspection and due diligence
8. Closing, deed, prorations, possession and walk-through
9. Default, mediation, earnest money disputes, termination, notice, and buyer's brokerage compensation

## Parties, property, inclusions and exclusions

- The **legal description** identifies the property. A street address alone is not enough.
- **Inclusions:** items attached to the property are included unless they are excluded. Examples are lighting, heating, plumbing, ventilating and air-conditioning units, built-in kitchen appliances, sprinkler systems and garage door openers. Some items are included whether or not they are attached, such as window coverings, storm windows, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors and all keys.
- Seller-owned solar panels, water softeners, security systems and satellite systems are included when they are checked.
- **Leased items** (for example, leased solar panels) and **encumbered inclusions** need the buyer's choice to assume (or not assume) the obligation, plus written approval from the lessor or lienholder before closing.
- Personal property is conveyed by **bill of sale** at closing.
- **Exclusions** are listed separately.
- **Water rights**, including deeded water rights, well rights and water stock, have their own subsection and a Water Rights Examination Deadline.

> **Exam tip:** If the seller wants to keep the dining-room chandelier, list it as an exclusion. Otherwise it's an attached fixture and it stays with the house.

## Purchase price and earnest money

The price table breaks the total into earnest money, new loan, assumption balance, private financing, seller financing and cash at closing. A **seller concession** is a credit to the buyer at closing that can cover costs the lender allows.

**Earnest money:**
- The buyer delivers it with the contract, unless the parties set an [[Alternative Earnest Money Deadline]].
- The [[Earnest Money Holder]] named in the contract keeps it in trust for both parties. It may be transferred to the closing company at or before closing.
- If the contract terminates and the buyer is entitled to the earnest money, the seller must sign the [[Earnest Money Release]] within **three days** of receiving it. If the seller is entitled, the buyer has the same three days. A party who doesn't sign in time is in default.

## Dates and Deadlines: how time works

The [[Dates and Deadlines]] table lists every deadline: title, association documents, disclosures, loan, appraisal, survey, inspection, closing and possession. The parties fill in either calendar dates or day counts from **[[MEC]]** (mutual execution of contract, the date both parties have signed).

### Counting rules

- **A "day" ends at 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time.**
- **To count a period of days, exclude the first day and include the last.** For "MEC + 3 days" when MEC is Monday, the deadline is Thursday.
- **The [[Time of Day Deadline]]** is optional. If it's filled in, it sets an earlier cutoff (for example, 5:00 p.m.) for objection, resolution, examination and termination deadlines. If it's blank, those deadlines also run to 11:59 p.m. MT.
- **Weekends and holidays:** a **Will / Will Not** checkbox decides whether a deadline that falls on a Saturday, Sunday or federal or Colorado state holiday moves to the next business day. **If neither box is checked, the deadline does not move.**
- **A blank, N/A or "Deleted" deadline** means that deadline and the provision tied to it don't apply.
- **[[Time is of the essence]]** for all dates and deadlines. A notice that arrives late is ineffective. In most cases, missing a termination deadline means you have waived that right.

> **Exam tip:** The weekend and holiday default is "not extended." A Saturday deadline stays on Saturday unless "Will" was checked.

### Acceptance

An offer expires unless both parties sign and the **offering party receives notice of acceptance** by the Acceptance Deadline Date and Time. Signing alone isn't enough. The offeror has to receive the notice.

## Financing conditions

The buyer selects the loan type (Conventional, FHA, VA, Bond or Other) and states whether verifiable funds are available for the cash at closing. The financing deadlines run in this order:

- **New Loan Application Deadline:** the buyer must have applied for the loan.
- **New Loan Terms Deadline:** the buyer may terminate if the loan terms are unsatisfactory, in the buyer's sole discretion.
- **[[New Loan Availability Deadline]]:** the buyer may terminate if the lender's underwriting result is unsatisfactory. This deadline can't be used for problems with the loan terms, the appraisal, insurability, lender property requirements or a conditional sale. Those have their own sections.

If the seller isn't in default and the buyer doesn't send a termination notice by the New Loan Availability Deadline, the **earnest money becomes nonrefundable**, except as the contract otherwise provides.

**Other financing paths:**
- **Seller's review of buyer credit:** the seller may evaluate the buyer's credit information and terminate by the Disapproval of Buyer's Credit Information Deadline.
- **Existing loan (assumption):** existing loan documents and lender transfer approval have their own deadlines.
- **Seller or private financing:** either party may terminate if the financing documents are unsatisfactory in that party's sole subjective discretion, by the Seller or Private Financing Deadline.

## Appraisal

The buyer or the buyer's lender orders the appraisal. The contract states who pays for it.

- The buyer may **terminate or object** by the **Appraisal Objection Deadline** if either of these happens:
  - The appraised value is less than the purchase price.
  - The appraisal isn't received by the **Appraisal Deadline**.
- An objection lets the parties negotiate, for example over a price reduction. If the objection isn't resolved by the **Appraisal Resolution Deadline**, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdraws the objection in writing first.
- **FHA and VA loans** have their own required appraisal language. The contract's appraisal deadlines don't apply to them.

> **Exam tip:** A low appraisal doesn't automatically end the contract. The buyer has to act by the Appraisal Objection Deadline, either by terminating or by objecting. If the buyer does nothing, that right is gone.

## Loan-related termination rights at a glance

| Problem | Deadline the buyer uses |
|---|---|
| Rate or terms unacceptable | New Loan Terms Deadline |
| Lender won't approve the loan | New Loan Availability Deadline |
| Appraisal low or late | Appraisal Objection Deadline |

lessons.title: The residential contract, part 2: title, disclosures, inspection, closing and default
lessons.body:
## Title: record and off-record

### Title insurance

- If neither box is checked, the **seller selects the title company and pays for the owner's policy**. The buyer may be the one to select instead, at the buyer's expense, if that option is chosen.
- [[Owner's Extended Coverage]] (OEC) is optional. It removes the standard exceptions for unrecorded matters such as parties in possession, unrecorded easements, survey matters and unrecorded mechanics' liens. The contract states who pays any added premium.

### Record title

By the **Record Title Deadline**, the seller delivers the title commitment and copies of the recorded exception documents. The buyer reviews them for [[record title]] problems and may object by the **Record Title Objection Deadline**. If documents arrive late or new exceptions appear, the buyer has until the earlier of closing or 10 days after receiving them. **A buyer who doesn't object accepts title as shown.**

### Off-record title

By the **Off-Record Title Deadline**, the seller delivers existing surveys and discloses known [[off-record title]] matters, such as unrecorded easements, boundary disputes and parties in possession. The buyer may inspect the property for these matters and object by the **Off-Record Title Objection Deadline**.

### Title resolution

If a title objection isn't resolved in writing by the **Title Resolution Deadline**, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdraws the objection in writing before the deadline.

### New ILC or survey

The contract states who orders and who pays for an [[Improvement Location Certificate]] (ILC) or survey. The buyer may terminate or object by the New ILC or New Survey Objection Deadline. If the objection isn't resolved, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdraws it.

## Owners' association

- At the seller's expense, by the Association Documents Deadline, the seller provides the [[association documents]]: governing documents, the list of insurance policies, assessments, financial documents and recent construction-defect notices.
- The buyer may terminate by the **Association Documents Termination Deadline**. If the documents are delivered late, the buyer gets 10 days after receipt.
- The seller requests the association [[status letter]] at least 14 days before closing and pays the status letter fee. The contract allocates other association fees, such as record-change fees and working-capital contributions, by checkbox.

## Seller disclosures

- **[[Seller's Property Disclosure]]:** the seller delivers the current Commission form by the Seller's Property Disclosure Deadline. The seller completes it from **current actual knowledge**. It is not a warranty, and the form itself says the seller fills it out, not the broker.
- **The duty is continuing.** The seller must disclose newly discovered adverse material facts. After such a disclosure, the buyer may terminate by the earlier of closing or 5 days after receiving it.
- **Lead-based paint:** required for dwellings built (or with a building permit issued) before January 1, 1978, with its own disclosure and termination deadlines.
- **Methamphetamine:** the seller discloses known manufacture, use or storage, unless the property was remediated to state standards.
- **Source of water:** the buyer acknowledges receiving the water source information, and well permit information if there's a well.
- **Carbon monoxide alarms:** if the home has a fuel-fired heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, plus a bedroom, Colorado law requires an operational alarm within 15 feet of each bedroom entrance (or where the building code requires).

## Inspection and objection/resolution

Inspection is the core due-diligence step. It has three deadlines that work together:

1. **Inspection Termination Deadline:** the buyer may simply terminate over any unsatisfactory condition, as long as the buyer hasn't already delivered an Inspection Objection.
2. **Inspection Objection Deadline:** the buyer delivers an [[Inspection Objection Notice]] listing the unsatisfactory items and the corrections requested.
3. **Inspection Resolution Deadline:** if the parties haven't signed a written agreement, usually the [[Inspection Resolution]] form, by this deadline, **the contract terminates**. The only way to avoid that is for the buyer to withdraw the objection in writing before the deadline.

The buyer pays for inspections, must repair any damage the inspections cause, and indemnifies the seller. These obligations survive termination.

> **Exam tip:** The resolution step works the opposite way from what students expect. **Silence kills the deal.** If nothing is agreed and the buyer doesn't withdraw the objection, the contract ends automatically at the Inspection Resolution Deadline.

### Other due-diligence items

- **Due diligence documents** (leases, leased-item and encumbered-inclusion documents, a septic permit if required) have their own delivery and objection deadlines.
- A **conditional sale** contingency makes the purchase depend on the buyer selling the property named in the contract. The buyer must terminate by the Conditional Sale Deadline or lose that right.

## Closing, deed and possession

- Closing happens on the Closing Date, or earlier by mutual agreement. The closing company prepares and delivers the closing documents under the Closing Instructions.
- **Deed:** if no other deed type is selected, the seller delivers a **special warranty deed**.
- **Possession** is delivered on the Possession Date and Time. A seller who holds over is subject to eviction and owes the per-day amount set in the contract plus actual damages. If the seller will stay after closing, a Post-Closing Occupancy Agreement controls possession.
- **Damage before closing:** if fire or another casualty damages the property and the damage is more than 10% of the purchase price, or the property isn't repaired before the Closing Date, the buyer may terminate. The buyer may walk through the property before closing.

## Prorations

Taxes, rents, water and sewer charges, propane and similar items are **prorated to the Closing Date**. For taxes, the parties choose the proration basis on the form, such as the prior calendar year's taxes or the most recent mill levy and assessed valuation. The basis can be adjusted for a qualifying seniors' or disabled-veteran exemption.

Rents are prorated on rents actually received. Security deposits transfer to the buyer. **Prorations are final** unless the Additional Provisions say otherwise.

> **Exam tip:** Colorado property taxes are paid in arrears. At closing, the seller gives the buyer a credit for the part of the year the seller owned the property, because the buyer will pay that year's bill the following year.

## Default and remedies

[[Time is of the essence]] for every deadline.

**If the buyer defaults**, the remedy depends on the specific performance checkbox:
- **Box not checked (the default):** [[liquidated damages]] apply. The seller keeps the earnest money as the seller's **only remedy**. The indemnity obligations (for inspection damage, for example) and attorney fees are the only exceptions.
- **Box checked:** the seller may cancel, keep the earnest money and recover other proper damages, **or** treat the contract as still in force and sue for [[specific performance]] and/or damages.

**If the seller defaults**, the buyer may:
- cancel, get the earnest money back and sue for damages, or
- sue for specific performance and/or damages.

The prevailing party in arbitration or litigation recovers reasonable costs and attorney fees.

## Mediation and earnest money disputes

- **[[Mediation]]** is required before arbitration or litigation. The parties choose the mediator together, split the cost equally, and the mediator's decision is not binding. The duty to mediate ends if the dispute isn't resolved within **30 days** of the written mediation request.
- **Earnest money dispute:** the Earnest Money Holder may hold the money until the dispute is settled or decided, interplead it into court, or notify the parties that it will return the money to the buyer unless it receives a court case number within **120 days**. The parties' duty to mediate still applies.

## Termination

A termination is effective when the other party **receives** a written [[Notice to Terminate]] by the applicable deadline. A late notice is ineffective, and that termination right is waived. When the contract terminates, the earnest money goes back to the buyer, unless the buyer is in default.

lessons.title: Counterproposals, amend/extend, notices and multiple offers
lessons.body:
## Counterproposal

When a seller wants different terms, the broker doesn't mark up the buyer's contract. The seller uses the Commission's **[[Counterproposal]]** form.

- The form references the proposed contract and lists only the changes: deadlines, price and financing terms, and "other changes."
- In the tables, a blank or "No Change" leaves a term as it was. "Deleted" removes the provision.
- **All other terms stay the same.**
- A new counterproposal **supersedes and replaces** any earlier one. The parties don't stack them.
- **Acceptance:** both parties sign, and the **offering party must receive notice of acceptance** by the deadline in the counterproposal. If that doesn't happen, the counterproposal expires.
- The form states that the party initiating the counterproposal does not sign the original contract itself.

Under general contract law, a counteroffer rejects the original offer. If the counterproposal expires, the buyer can't go back and accept the original offer, because that offer is gone.

> **Exam tip:** Who has to *receive* notice of acceptance? The party who made the latest offer or counterproposal. A counterproposal that is signed but never communicated hasn't been accepted.

## Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract

After the contract is signed, changes to it require the **[[Agreement to Amend/Extend]]**.

- Both parties sign. A broker can't change a deadline on their own authority.
- The form's table lists the contract's deadlines (new date, "No Change" or "Deleted"), with room for other amendments.
- All other terms remain the same.
- Like a counterproposal, it has an acceptance deadline. It expires if notice of acceptance isn't received in time.

**Typical uses:**
- Moving the closing date because the lender needs more time.
- Changing the price after an appraisal negotiation.
- Extending the Inspection Resolution Deadline while the parties keep negotiating. This has to be signed **before** the deadline passes, or the contract may already have terminated.

### Related forms new for 2026

- **Agreement to Revive Contract:** brings back a contract that has already terminated. The parties state the termination date, ratify the contract, and set new deadlines. The seller represents that no other sale contract is in effect.
- **Extension or Termination of Contract:** one party proposes extending deadlines in Part I. If both parties don't sign Part I and receive notice of acceptance in time, Part II works as the requesting party's notice to terminate, based on the contract provisions checked.

> **Exam tip:** A contract terminated at the Inspection Resolution Deadline can't be amended, because there's nothing left to amend. The parties use the Agreement to Revive Contract or write a new contract.

## Inspection, title and appraisal notices

The Commission publishes notice forms so that deadline-driven steps are in writing:

| Form | Who sends it | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Inspection Objection Notice | Buyer | Lists unsatisfactory items and corrections wanted |
| Inspection Resolution | Buyer and seller sign | Seller agrees to specific corrections at seller's expense. Amends the contract. |
| Title-Related Objection Notice (renamed Title, Survey and Due Diligence-Related Objection Notice in the 2027 version) | Buyer | Objects to title, survey or association matters |
| Appraised Value Objection Notice | Buyer | Objects to a low or missing appraisal |
| Notice to Terminate | Either party | Ends the contract under a specific provision |
| Earnest Money Release | Buyer and seller sign | Directs the holder how to pay out the earnest money and mutually releases the parties |

The buyer should give a copy of an Inspection Resolution to the lender. Repairs or credits can change the loan.

## Notice and delivery

- Notices must be **in writing**.
- A notice is effective when **received**, not when sent.
- Delivery to the party's broker or brokerage firm counts as delivery to the party, **except** notices after closing, which must be received by the party. For electronic notice, the form adds notices after cancellation or termination to that exception.
- **Electronic notice** is allowed through the methods the parties list, such as email or fax.
- **Electronic delivery** of documents is allowed by email, by a link or website, or by fax.
- The contract may be signed in **counterparts**. Each party may sign a separate copy.
- Colorado law governs the contract.

> **Exam tip:** The buyer emails a Notice to Terminate at 11:50 p.m. on the deadline, and it reaches the seller's broker's inbox at 11:52 p.m. Mountain Time. It's timely, because receipt by the broker counts. If the contract has a 5:00 p.m. Time of Day Deadline, the same email is late.

## Multiple offers in Colorado practice

Colorado has no special multiple-offer form. The rules come from agency duties and the listing contract:

- **Present every offer.** A seller's agent must present all offers to and from the seller in a timely manner, **even when the property is already under contract** (C.R.S. 12-10-404). The Division has warned that a listing broker can't refuse an offer because the buyer's broker used different contract software or works under a different compensation model.
- **Limits must be in writing.** A listing broker may limit which offers are presented only after explaining the pros and cons to the seller, and the limit has to be written into the listing contract.
- **If the listing broker won't respond:** the buyer's broker goes to the listing broker's employing broker, and only after that fails, to the seller directly.
- **Disclosing other offers:** the Exclusive Right-to-Sell contract has a box for whether the seller **does or does not** consent to disclosing that other offers exist. **If neither box is checked, there is no consent.** Disclosing the **terms** of an offer always requires the seller's written consent.
- **Confidential:** without the seller's informed consent, the seller's agent may not disclose that the seller would take less than the asking price, or the seller's motivations.
- **Under contract:** once the property is under contract, the listing broker doesn't have to keep looking for offers, but still presents any that come in. A seller who accepts a second offer should make it a backup offer that depends on the first contract terminating. Otherwise the seller risks two binding contracts.

### Running a multiple-offer round

1. Confirm the seller's instructions about disclosing that other offers exist.
2. Treat all buyers' brokers the same way, for example the same "highest and best by Friday at 5 p.m." message.
3. Present every offer to the seller.
4. Use a Counterproposal to respond to one offer. Countering several buyers at once can create more than one binding contract if more than one accepts, so that strategy needs care and usually a lawyer.

lessons.title: Listing and buyer agreements, disclosures, addenda, closing and seller financing
lessons.body:
## Exclusive Right-to-Sell Listing Contract

The listing contract sets up the brokerage relationship between the seller and the firm.

- **Relationship:** the seller chooses **seller agency** or **transaction-brokerage**. If neither box is checked, the broker is a **transaction-broker**.
- **Listing period:** from the start date to the earlier of a completed sale or the end date, plus any written extensions. The contract is "exclusive" and "irrevocable," but either side may cancel in writing if the other fails to substantially perform.
- **Compensation is negotiable.** It can be a percentage of the gross price or a flat dollar amount, with separate terms for a lease if leasing is authorized. It is earned in any of these situations:
  - The property sells during the listing period, **by anyone**, including the seller.
  - The broker finds a buyer who is ready, willing and able to buy on the listing terms.
  - A sale closes in the holdover period to a submitted prospect.
- **Cooperation:** the listing firm may share its compensation with a buyer's brokerage firm. Any limit on offers or any choice about disclosing offers goes into the listing contract in writing.
- **Third-party compensation:** the broker may not accept it without the seller's written consent.
- **Earnest money:** the firm may accept it and deliver it to the closing agent.
- **Seller duties:** whether the seller will provide a Seller's Property Disclosure, lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 homes, and carbon monoxide alarms in place before the property is offered for sale.
- **Disputes:** mediation is required (30 days), and the prevailing party gets attorney fees.

### Holdover period

The [[holdover period]] protects the firm from a seller and buyer who wait out the listing to avoid paying the commission.

- It is a stated number of days after the listing expires.
- It covers sales to a **[[Submitted Prospect]]**, meaning a person the broker negotiated with and whose name was given to the seller **in writing during the listing period**.
- **The double-commission checkbox:** a **Will / Will Not** box decides whether the seller still owes this firm if the seller signs a new exclusive listing with another firm during the holdover period and that firm earns a commission on the sale to the Submitted Prospect. **If neither box is checked, the seller does not owe this firm** in that situation.
- If no new listing is involved, a sale to a Submitted Prospect within the holdover period earns the compensation.

> **Exam tip:** The holdover clause only covers names the broker submitted **in writing** before the listing expired. A buyer the broker showed the house to but never named in writing isn't covered.

## Exclusive Right-to-Buy Contract

The buyer-side counterpart:

- **Buyer agency or transaction-brokerage.** If neither box is checked, the broker is a **transaction-broker**.
- **Compensation is negotiable and not set by law.** It can be a success fee, an hourly fee or a retainer. Amounts paid by the seller or the listing firm count toward it. The buyer owes any unpaid balance only if the broker disclosed that amount in writing before the buyer signed a contract with the seller.
- **Holdover** covers properties the broker negotiated and described to the buyer **in writing** during the listing period. A Will / Will Not box decides whether the buyer still owes this firm if another firm, under a new exclusive signed during holdover, earns compensation. If no box is checked, the buyer doesn't owe it.
- The broker may show the same properties to other buyers.
- The buyer must refer all inquiries about properties to the broker.
- The contract includes wire-fraud warnings: verify wiring instructions by phone using a number you know is genuine, not one taken from the email.

## Disclosure documents

| Form | Who completes it | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| [[Seller's Property Disclosure]] | **Seller**, not the broker | Current actual knowledge. Not a warranty. Covers structure, roof, systems, water and sewer, environmental issues including radon, HOA, metro district, and more |
| [[Square Footage Disclosure]] | **Listing licensee** | States whether the licensee measured, which standard was used, and other sources (prior appraisal, plans, assessor). Marketing only. The buyer should measure independently by the contract deadline if size matters |
| [[Source of Water Addendum]] | Seller | Well (permit number), water provider (contact information), or some other source. Warns that some providers rely on nonrenewable groundwater |
| [[Lead-Based Paint Disclosure]] | Seller, with licensees | Pre-1978 housing. EPA pamphlet. Buyer gets a 10-day risk-assessment opportunity, which can be changed or waived in writing. Licensees must make sure the rules are followed. Seller keeps a copy for 3 years |

The broker still has a separate duty to disclose adverse material facts the broker actually knows. The seller's form doesn't replace that duty.

> **Exam tip:** If the seller asks the listing broker to fill out the Seller's Property Disclosure "since you know the house," the broker should decline. The seller completes it from the seller's own knowledge.

> **Check the current form:** the listing contracts, Short Sale Addenda, Source of Water Addendum, lead-based paint forms, notes and deeds of trust all have substantive revisions mandatory January 1, 2027. The rules below are from the 2026 versions.

## Addenda

### Short Sale Addendum

Use it when the seller's liens are more than the sale price, so lienholders must agree to accept less.

- The seller submits the contract package to each lienholder by a deadline.
- If written lienholder acceptance doesn't arrive by the **Short Sale Acceptance Deadline**, the contract terminates.
- After acceptance, the seller may terminate within 3 days if the lienholder's terms are unacceptable to the seller. The buyer may terminate within 3 days if the contract changes the acceptance requires (made by Amend/Extend) are unacceptable to the buyer.
- Changing deadlines still requires an Agreement to Amend/Extend. Material changes may need to be resubmitted to the lender.
- The seller may still owe the deficiency unless the lender releases it in writing, and forgiven debt can be taxable. The form strongly urges legal and tax advice.

### Residential contract under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act

Use this contract instead of CBS1 when all of these are true:
- the property is in foreclosure, or the buyer knows a loan is at least 30 days delinquent,
- the seller lives in the property as a principal residence, and
- the buyer will not live there. The buyer is an [[equity purchaser]].

The Commission form can't be used if the deal includes a loan assumption, a leaseback to the seller or a repurchase option. An attorney has to prepare that contract. When the form is used:
- A Notice of Cancellation and a Seller Warning are attached.
- The seller receives nothing of value until the cancellation right expires.
- If the seller's principal language isn't English, a translated Homeowner Warning Notice is also required.

By statute, the homeowner may cancel until the **earlier** of midnight of the **third business day** after signing or noon on the day before the foreclosure sale. The Act doesn't apply when a Short Sale Addendum is part of the contract.

## Closing Instructions

The [[Closing Instructions]] are signed by the **buyer, the seller and the closing company**. They engage the closing company to:

- prepare the closing documents. That includes standard statutory deeds (general warranty, special warranty, bargain and sale, quitclaim). Personal representative's deeds, trustee's deeds and deeds with nonstandard exceptions must come from the parties or their attorneys.
- prepare accurate closing statements.
- record documents and disburse funds only after receiving **good funds**.
- handle FIRPTA and Colorado withholding.

Changing the instructions requires a writing signed by all three. If closing doesn't happen by the Closing Date, documents and money go back to whoever deposited them.

## Seller financing: notes and deeds of trust

When the seller carries back financing, the price table shows the seller-financed amount, and either party may terminate if the financing documents are unsatisfactory, by the Seller or Private Financing Deadline. The Commission provides:

- **[[Promissory note]]** forms, including a Promissory Note for Deed of Trust. It has blanks for the rate, payments, maturity, late charge and default rate. Prepayment is allowed without penalty unless the form says otherwise, and the holder may accelerate on default.
- **[[Deed of trust]]** forms in three versions:
  - **Due on Transfer – Strict**
  - **Due on Transfer – Creditworthy:** the lender may accelerate if the person the property is transferred to isn't creditworthy.
  - **Assumable – Not Due on Transfer**

The [[Public Trustee]] of the county is the trustee. Releasing the deed of trust through the Public Trustee generally requires the original note (or a substitute the release statute allows).

**What brokers may do:** fill in the blanks on these Commission-approved forms, in a transaction they are brokering, with no extra fee.

**What brokers may not do:**
- Advise which due-on-transfer version or default terms are legally best for a party.
- Draft custom financing terms.
- Prepare documents for a deal they aren't brokering.

The forms themselves warn that if the loan is a **consumer credit transaction**, the parties should consult legal counsel. That is a strong signal to bring in an attorney.

questions.stem: A broker is listing a four-unit apartment building that the owner rents to tenants. Which Commission-approved sales contract is the best fit?
choices: Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Income-Residential)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Land)
Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Commercial) with no addendum
questions.explanation: Income-producing residential property, whether 1–4 units or larger, uses the Income-Residential contract. It has provisions for leases, rent rolls, tenant estoppel statements and security deposits that the Residential contract isn't built around.

questions.stem: Under C.R.S. 12-10-403(4), when MUST a Colorado broker use a Commission-approved form?
choices: Only in residential transactions, not commercial or land deals
Only when the buyer is not represented by a Colorado attorney
Whenever one exists and is appropriate for the transaction
Only when the broker is acting as a single agent for a party
questions.explanation: The statute requires a Commission-approved form whenever one exists and is appropriate. Other standard forms, such as attorney-drafted or party-provided forms, are allowed only in the circumstances the law permits.

questions.stem: A buyer asks his broker to write a detailed clause in Additional Provisions that sets out which party bears liability if a neighbor's boundary fence is later found to encroach. What should the broker do?
choices: Draft the clause, since Additional Provisions are not Commission-approved anyway
Copy a similar clause from one of the broker's previous transactions
Refuse to include any language about the fence in the contract
Recommend that an attorney draft it, since drafting it is the practice of law
questions.explanation: Brokers may record simple agreed facts but may not draft legal provisions that allocate rights and liabilities. An attorney should draft that language, and the broker must understand any attorney-drafted clause before using it.

questions.stem: The Conway-Bogue decision allowed Colorado brokers to complete standard forms under certain conditions. Which condition is part of that holding?
choices: No charge for the documents beyond the ordinary commission
The broker must also hold a Colorado law license
The broker may prepare deeds for friends as a favor
The broker may draft custom contracts if both parties consent
questions.explanation: Conway-Bogue (1957) let brokers fill in standard forms only in transactions they are brokering and with no compensation beyond their ordinary commission. Preparing documents as a favor in other transactions or drafting custom contracts is not permitted.

questions.stem: A contract's Dates and Deadlines table sets the Inspection Objection Deadline as "MEC + 5 days." Mutual execution occurred on a Tuesday. On which day does the deadline fall?
choices: Saturday
Monday
Friday
Sunday
questions.explanation: Exclude the first day (Tuesday) and include the last: Wednesday is 1, Thursday 2, Friday 3, Saturday 4, Sunday 5. Whether a Sunday deadline moves to Monday depends on the weekend/holiday Will/Will Not box.

questions.stem: A Colorado residential contract deadline falls on a Sunday. Neither box in the weekend/holiday extension provision is checked, and no Time of Day Deadline applies. When does the deadline expire?
choices: 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time on the following Monday
11:59 p.m. Mountain Time on that Sunday
5:00 p.m. Mountain Time on the preceding Friday
Noon on that Sunday
questions.explanation: If neither box is checked, a deadline that falls on a weekend or holiday is not extended. A day ends at 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time unless a Time of Day Deadline applies to that type of deadline.

questions.stem: The parties enter 5:00 p.m. as the Time of Day Deadline in the Colorado residential contract. Which deadline does that time apply to?
choices: The Closing Date and the time of closing
The Possession Date and Possession Time
The Inspection Objection Deadline
The Acceptance Deadline Date and Time
questions.explanation: The Time of Day Deadline applies to objection, resolution, examination and termination deadlines, such as the Inspection Objection Deadline. Possession and acceptance have their own times in the Dates and Deadlines table, and closing is set by the Closing Date.

questions.stem: A buyer signs the seller's counterproposal at 4:00 p.m. on the acceptance deadline but doesn't tell anyone until the next morning. The counterproposal required acceptance by 6:00 p.m. that day. What is the result?
choices: It expired; the seller never received notice of acceptance in time
A binding contract formed at 4:00 p.m., when the buyer signed
A contract formed because signing came before the 6:00 p.m. deadline
The buyer's original offer revives and binds the seller
questions.explanation: Acceptance requires that the offering party receive notice of acceptance by the deadline. Signing without timely notice doesn't form a contract. The original offer was rejected by the counterproposal and is not revived.

questions.stem: A seller sends a second counterproposal to a buyer before the buyer responds to the first one. What effect does the second counterproposal have?
choices: Both counterproposals are open and the buyer may accept either
It supersedes and replaces the earlier counterproposal
It is invalid without the buyer's consent
It converts the transaction to an Agreement to Amend/Extend
questions.explanation: The Commission's Counterproposal states that it supersedes and replaces any previous counterproposal. Only the latest one can be accepted.

questions.stem: After the contract is fully signed, the lender says it needs an extra week before closing. What should the brokers use to change the Closing Date?
choices: A Counterproposal signed by the seller and sent to the buyer
A new Contract to Buy and Sell replacing the original one
An Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract signed by both parties
A written memo from the listing broker to the closing company
questions.explanation: Changes to a signed contract's dates are made with the Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract, signed by both parties, with notice of acceptance received by its deadline. Brokers can't change deadlines on their own.

questions.stem: A buyer delivers a timely Inspection Objection Notice. The Inspection Resolution Deadline passes with no signed agreement, and the buyer has not withdrawn the objection. What happens?
choices: The contract terminates
Seller must make the repairs
The contract continues as written
Buyer must close, then sue
questions.explanation: Under the Colorado contract, if the parties haven't resolved an inspection objection in writing by the Inspection Resolution Deadline, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdrew the objection in writing before the deadline.

questions.stem: A buyer wants to walk away after an inspection, without negotiating repairs. Which deadline should the buyer use?
choices: Inspection Resolution Deadline
Inspection Termination Deadline
Due Diligence Documents Objection Deadline
New Loan Terms Deadline
questions.explanation: The Inspection Termination Deadline lets the buyer terminate outright over an unsatisfactory condition, as long as the buyer hasn't already delivered an Inspection Objection. The objection and resolution deadlines are for negotiating corrections.

questions.stem: The buyer's appraisal comes in $15,000 below the purchase price on a conventional loan. Which statement is correct under the Colorado residential contract?
choices: The contract terminates automatically at the Appraisal Resolution Deadline
The seller must reduce the price to match the appraised value
The buyer may terminate or object by the Appraisal Objection Deadline
The buyer must close and pay the $15,000 difference in cash
questions.explanation: A low or late appraisal gives the buyer the right to terminate or object by the Appraisal Objection Deadline. Nothing happens automatically. If the buyer doesn't act, the right is lost.

questions.stem: Which loan types have their own appraisal language, so the contract's appraisal deadlines don't apply to them?
choices: Conventional and bond loans
Seller-carry and private loans
Jumbo loans
FHA and VA loans
questions.explanation: The Colorado contract notes that the appraisal deadlines don't apply to FHA-insured or VA-guaranteed loans, which carry their own required appraisal provisions.

questions.stem: A buyer's lender denies the loan, but the buyer doesn't deliver a Notice to Terminate by the New Loan Availability Deadline. The seller is not in default. What is the likely consequence?
choices: The earnest money becomes nonrefundable, except as the contract provides
The contract automatically terminates and all earnest money goes back to the buyer
The seller must extend the deadline
The closing company must refund the earnest money
questions.explanation: If the buyer doesn't timely terminate under the New Loan Availability provision and the seller isn't in default, the earnest money becomes nonrefundable, except as the contract otherwise provides. Time is of the essence.

questions.stem: The Colorado residential contract has no title-company box checked. Who selects the title insurance company and pays for the owner's policy?
choices: The buyer, at the buyer's expense
The seller, at the seller's expense
The listing broker, with costs split equally
The buyer's lender
questions.explanation: If neither box is checked, the seller-selects option applies: the seller selects the title company and pays for the owner's title insurance policy.

questions.stem: A buyer reviews the title commitment and does not object by the Record Title Objection Deadline. What is the effect?
choices: The seller must still remove all exceptions before closing
The buyer may object at closing
The contract terminates
The buyer accepts the condition of title as disclosed
questions.explanation: A buyer who doesn't deliver a timely title objection accepts title as shown. Objections must be received by the deadline because time is of the essence.

questions.stem: Which matter is an off-record title issue the buyer would look for during the Off-Record Title period?
choices: A recorded deed of trust securing the seller's loan
An unrecorded easement shown by a path neighbors use
A recorded subdivision plat showing utility easements
A recorded HOA declaration with use restrictions
questions.explanation: Off-record matters don't appear in the public records. Examples are unrecorded easements, boundary disputes and parties in possession. Recorded documents are reviewed under record title.

questions.stem: A buyer timely objects to an easement shown on the title commitment. The seller doesn't respond, and no written resolution exists by the Title Resolution Deadline. The buyer hasn't withdrawn the objection. What happens?
choices: The contract terminates
Buyer takes title subject to it
Seller is in default and owes damages
Closing is delayed 10 days
questions.explanation: Unresolved title objections work like inspection objections. If there's no written resolution by the Title Resolution Deadline, the contract terminates unless the buyer withdrew the objection first.

questions.stem: Who pays the fee for the owners' association status letter under the Colorado residential contract?
choices: The buyer
The buyer and seller equally
The seller
The listing brokerage firm
questions.explanation: The residential contract makes the seller pay any fee for issuing the association's status letter. Other association fees, such as record-change or working-capital fees, are allocated by checkbox.

questions.stem: A seller asks the listing broker to complete the Seller's Property Disclosure because the broker has seen the house many times. What is the best response?
choices: Complete it, since the broker's observations are more reliable than the seller's
Complete it, then have the seller review and sign it
Leave it blank and let the buyer's inspection cover it
Explain that the seller must complete it from the seller's own knowledge
questions.explanation: The Commission's form is completed by the seller, not the broker, based on the seller's current actual knowledge. The broker separately discloses adverse material facts the broker knows.

questions.stem: Two weeks after delivering the Seller's Property Disclosure, the seller discovers a crack in the foundation. What must happen under the residential contract?
choices: Nothing, because the Seller's Property Disclosure Deadline has passed
The seller may wait and mention it at the closing table
The seller must disclose it, and the buyer gets a short right to terminate
The listing broker decides whether the crack is material enough to disclose
questions.explanation: The seller has a continuing duty to disclose newly discovered adverse material facts. The buyer may then terminate by the earlier of closing or 5 days after receiving the disclosure.

questions.stem: The specific performance box in the buyer-default section is NOT checked, and the buyer defaults. What is the seller's remedy?
choices: The seller may sue for specific performance to force the buyer to close
The seller may keep the earnest money and also sue for actual damages
Seller keeps the earnest money as liquidated damages, its only remedy
The seller must return the earnest money to the buyer and relist
questions.explanation: Unless the specific performance box is checked, liquidated damages apply. The earnest money is the seller's only remedy for buyer default, apart from the buyer's inspection indemnity and the legal-fee provision.

questions.stem: The seller refuses to close on a valid contract, and the buyer is ready to perform. Which remedy is available to the buyer?
choices: Specific performance and/or damages
Only return of the earnest money
Only liquidated damages equal to twice the earnest money
No remedy until mediation is waived by the seller
questions.explanation: If the seller defaults, the buyer may cancel, recover the earnest money and seek damages, or seek specific performance and/or damages. Mediation must be attempted first but doesn't eliminate these remedies.

questions.stem: A dispute arises over who gets the earnest money after a failed transaction. What must the parties do before filing a lawsuit or arbitration, under the residential contract?
choices: Nothing; either party may sue or demand arbitration immediately
Submit the dispute to binding arbitration administered by the title company
Ask the Real Estate Commission to hold a hearing and decide it
Attempt mediation, which ends if unresolved 30 days after the request
questions.explanation: The contract requires good-faith mediation before arbitration or litigation. Costs are split equally, and the duty to mediate ends if the dispute isn't resolved within 30 days of the written mediation request.

questions.stem: The buyer properly terminated and the seller has received an Earnest Money Release. How long does the seller have to sign it before being in default?
choices: 3 days after receipt
10 days after receipt
30 days after receipt
120 days after receipt
questions.explanation: The contract requires the party entitled to sign the earnest money release instructions to do so within three days of receiving them. Not signing on time is a default.

questions.stem: Buyer and seller each claim the earnest money and won't sign a release. The Earnest Money Holder sends a notice under the contract's dispute provision. If no court case number is received in time, the holder may return the money to the buyer. How long is that period?
choices: 30 days
60 days
120 days
180 days
questions.explanation: Under the earnest money dispute provision, the holder may return the earnest money to the buyer unless it receives a case number within 120 days of its notice to the parties. The holder may also wait or interplead the funds.

questions.stem: A buyer's Notice to Terminate arrives one day after the applicable termination deadline. What is the effect?
choices: It is effective because it was mailed before the deadline
It is ineffective, and that termination right is waived
It is effective if the seller has not yet closed
It extends the deadline automatically
questions.explanation: Termination is effective on the other party's receipt of a written notice by the deadline. A late notice is ineffective and the right is waived, because time is of the essence.

questions.stem: Under the Colorado residential contract, delivery of a notice to which person counts as delivery to the seller before closing?
choices: Only the seller personally, at the seller's address
The title company handling the closing
The buyer's lender or mortgage broker
The seller's broker or brokerage firm
questions.explanation: Before closing, a notice is effective when received by the party or by the broker or brokerage firm working with that party. Notices after closing (and electronic notices after cancellation or termination) must be received by the party itself.

questions.stem: No deed type is selected in the residential contract. What deed must the seller deliver at closing?
choices: General warranty deed
Quitclaim deed
Special warranty deed
Bargain and sale deed
questions.explanation: If no other deed is selected, the seller must deliver a good and sufficient special warranty deed.

questions.stem: A listing expired. Ten days later, the seller sells directly to a buyer the listing broker had negotiated with and named to the seller in writing during the listing. The listing has a 60-day holdover period, and the seller has not signed a listing with any other firm. Is compensation owed?
choices: No, because compensation is earned only during the listing period
Yes, because the buyer is a Submitted Prospect and the sale is in holdover
Only if the buyer had also signed an exclusive right-to-buy contract
No, because the seller, not the broker, negotiated the final sale after expiration
questions.explanation: The holdover clause covers a sale during the holdover period to a person the broker negotiated with and named to the seller in writing during the listing period. The Will/Will Not box only matters when another firm earns a commission under a new exclusive listing signed during the holdover, which didn't happen here.

questions.stem: In the Exclusive Right-to-Sell Listing Contract, neither box is checked on whether the seller consents to disclosing the existence of offers. A buyer's broker asks whether there are other offers. What may the listing broker do?
choices: Disclose how many offers there are, but not their prices or terms
Disclose the terms if the buyer's broker promises to keep them confidential
Disclose everything, since multiple offers are public information
Decline to disclose that offers exist, since the seller hasn't consented
questions.explanation: If neither box is checked, the seller does not consent to disclosing that offers exist. Disclosing the terms of any offer always requires the seller's written consent.

questions.stem: A property is under contract, and the listing broker receives another written offer. What must the seller's agent do?
choices: Present it to the seller in a timely manner
Hold it until the first contract fails
Return it, because the property is under contract
Present it only if it is higher than the existing contract price
questions.explanation: Colorado law and the listing contract require a seller's agent to present all offers in a timely manner, even when the property is under contract. A seller who accepts should make it a backup contract.

questions.stem: Which Commission-approved document is completed by the listing licensee and states the measurement source and that square footage is for marketing purposes only?
choices: Seller's Property Disclosure
Square Footage Disclosure
Source of Water Addendum
Closing Instructions
questions.explanation: The Square Footage Disclosure is completed by the listing licensee. It identifies whether the licensee measured, the standard used, and other sources, and it warns the buyer to measure independently if exact size matters.

questions.stem: A homeowner in foreclosure who lives in the home agrees to sell it to an investor who will not live there. No short sale is involved. Which contract is required?
choices: The standard Residential contract with a Short Sale Addendum attached
The Land contract with a Residential Addendum
The Residential (Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act) contract
An attorney-drafted contract only
questions.explanation: When the seller occupies the home as a principal residence, the buyer won't occupy it, and the buyer knows the seller is in default or at least 30 days delinquent (as in foreclosure), the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act version of the residential contract applies. It comes with a Seller Warning and Notice of Cancellation. A short sale would instead use the standard contract with a Short Sale Addendum.

questions.stem: Under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act, how long does a homeowner who signs a contract with an equity purchaser have to cancel?
choices: Midnight of the 3rd business day after signing or noon the day before the sale, whichever is earlier
Until 10 calendar days after signing, or until closing if that comes first
Midnight of the 5th business day after signing or the day of the sale, whichever is later
Until 30 days after the foreclosure sale, during the redemption period
questions.explanation: C.R.S. 6-1-1113 lets the homeowner cancel until the earlier of midnight of the third business day after signing or noon on the day before the foreclosure sale.

questions.stem: A seller will carry back a note from the buyer. What may the broker who is handling the sale do?
choices: Draft custom default and acceleration terms if the seller has no attorney
Fill in the Commission-approved note and deed of trust forms, with no extra fee
Charge a separate document-preparation fee for the note and the deed of trust
Act as the lender of record so the seller financing is properly documented
questions.explanation: Under the forms statute and Conway-Bogue, a broker may complete Commission-approved notes and deeds of trust in a transaction the broker is handling, with no charge beyond the commission. Custom drafting requires an attorney, and the forms themselves warn the parties to consult counsel if it's a consumer credit transaction.

questions.stem: Who signs the Commission-approved Closing Instructions?
choices: Buyer, seller and the closing company
The listing broker and the buyer's broker
Only the buyer's lender and the closing company
Buyer and seller only
questions.explanation: Buyer, seller and the closing company sign the Closing Instructions, which engage the closing company for closing and settlement services. Changing them requires a writing signed by all three.

cards.front: Statute letting Colorado brokers complete standard forms
cards.back: C.R.S. 12-10-403(4): a broker acting as a single agent or transaction-broker may complete standard forms.

cards.front: When must a Commission-approved form be used?
cards.back: Whenever one exists and is appropriate for the transaction.

cards.front: Warning a broker must give whenever forms are used
cards.back: The forms have important legal consequences, and the parties should consult legal counsel before signing.

cards.front: Conway-Bogue (1957): conditions for brokers filling in forms
cards.back: Standard forms only, only in transactions where they act as broker, and no fee beyond the ordinary commission.

cards.front: Party-provided or lender-required form: broker's limit
cards.back: Insert transaction-specific information only.

cards.front: Party-provided form: record the broker must keep
cards.back: Written confirmation of who provided the form.

cards.front: Letter of intent requirement
cards.back: It must state on its face that it is nonbinding.

cards.front: Deleting printed text on a Commission form
cards.back: Only because of negotiation or a party's instruction. Strike through so it stays legible.

cards.front: Inapplicable section of a form
cards.back: Keep the caption and mark it omitted or not applicable.

cards.front: Additional Provisions: what belongs there
cards.back: Agreed terms from negotiation or party instructions. No broker legal drafting and no exculpatory clauses for the broker. Keep attorney-drafted clauses 4 years.

cards.front: Broker-principal using their own attorney's form
cards.back: Allowed, but it must conspicuously state that it is not a Commission-approved form.

cards.front: Commission-approved leases or property management agreements?
cards.back: None exist.

cards.front: Contract for a duplex or fourplex held as a rental
cards.back: Income-Residential (CBS2).

cards.front: Contract for a retail strip center
cards.back: Commercial (CBS3). Attach the Residential Addendum if there are residences.

cards.front: Contract for vacant acreage
cards.back: Land (CBS4): growing crops, water rights, mineral rights.

cards.front: What does MEC mean?
cards.back: Mutual execution of contract: the date both parties have signed.

cards.front: When does a contract "day" end?
cards.back: 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time.

cards.front: Counting a period of days
cards.back: Exclude the first day and include the last.

cards.front: Weekend or holiday deadline with neither box checked
cards.back: Not extended. The deadline stays on the weekend or holiday.

cards.front: Which deadlines does the Time of Day Deadline cover?
cards.back: Objection, resolution, examination and termination deadlines.

cards.front: Deadline left blank, N/A or "Deleted"
cards.back: That deadline and its related provision don't apply.

cards.front: When is an offer accepted?
cards.back: Both parties sign, and the offering party receives notice of acceptance by the Acceptance Deadline.

cards.front: When is earnest money due?
cards.back: With the contract, unless there is an Alternative Earnest Money Deadline.

cards.front: Time to sign the Earnest Money Release after receiving it
cards.back: 3 days. Not signing on time is a default.

cards.front: Who signs the Earnest Money Release form?
cards.back: Buyer and seller (no broker signature lines).

cards.front: Missing the New Loan Availability Deadline (seller not in default)
cards.back: Earnest money becomes nonrefundable, except as the contract otherwise provides.

cards.front: Low or late appraisal: buyer's options
cards.back: Terminate or object by the Appraisal Objection Deadline.

cards.front: Appraisal deadlines and FHA/VA
cards.back: They don't apply. FHA and VA use their own appraisal language.

cards.front: Title company selection if no box is checked
cards.back: Seller selects the title company and pays for the owner's policy.

cards.front: No title objection by the deadline
cards.back: The buyer accepts title as shown.

cards.front: Late title documents: buyer's objection window
cards.back: The earlier of closing or 10 days after receipt.

cards.front: Examples of off-record title matters
cards.back: Unrecorded easements, boundary disputes, parties in possession.

cards.front: What OEC covers
cards.back: Owner's Extended Coverage removes the standard exceptions for unrecorded matters (possession, unrecorded easements, survey matters, unrecorded mechanics' liens).

cards.front: Who pays for the association documents?
cards.back: The seller.

cards.front: Status letter: when requested and who pays
cards.back: Requested at least 14 days before closing. The seller pays the status letter fee.

cards.front: Who completes the Seller's Property Disclosure, and on what standard?
cards.back: The seller, from current actual knowledge. It is not a warranty.

cards.front: Newly discovered adverse fact after disclosure
cards.back: Seller must disclose it. Buyer may terminate by the earlier of closing or 5 days after receipt.

cards.front: Inspection: three deadlines in order
cards.back: Termination, Objection, Resolution.

cards.front: Inspection objection unresolved at the Resolution Deadline
cards.back: The contract terminates unless the buyer withdrew the objection in writing first.

cards.front: Who pays for inspections and for damage they cause?
cards.back: The buyer, who also indemnifies the seller. These obligations survive termination.

cards.front: Lead-based paint: which dwellings?
cards.back: Built, or permitted, before January 1, 1978.

cards.front: Default deed if none is selected
cards.back: Special warranty deed.

cards.front: Property damage before closing: when may the buyer terminate?
cards.back: If the damage exceeds 10% of the purchase price, or the property isn't repaired before the Closing Date.

cards.front: Proration date in the residential contract
cards.back: Prorated to the Closing Date. Prorations are final unless Additional Provisions say otherwise.

cards.front: Buyer default, specific performance box not checked
cards.back: Liquidated damages: the seller keeps the earnest money as the only remedy (except indemnity and legal fees).

cards.front: Seller default: buyer's remedies
cards.back: Cancel, get earnest money back and seek damages, OR seek specific performance and/or damages.

cards.front: Mediation requirement
cards.back: Required before arbitration or litigation. Costs split equally. Duty ends if not resolved within 30 days of the written request.

cards.front: Earnest money dispute: holder's options
cards.back: Wait, interplead, or return the money to the buyer if no case number arrives within 120 days of its notice.

cards.front: When is termination effective?
cards.back: On the other party's receipt of a written Notice to Terminate by the deadline.

cards.front: Is notice to the broker notice to the party?
cards.back: Yes, before closing. After closing (and, for electronic notice, after cancellation or termination) the party must receive it.

cards.front: Counterproposal: effect on earlier counterproposals
cards.back: It supersedes and replaces them. Terms not changed stay the same.

cards.front: Form for changing deadlines after the contract is signed
cards.back: Agreement to Amend/Extend Contract, signed by both parties.

cards.front: Form for bringing a terminated contract back
cards.back: Agreement to Revive Contract.

cards.front: Holdover period: who is covered?
cards.back: Submitted Prospects: persons the broker negotiated with and named to the seller in writing during the listing period.

cards.front: Listing holdover Will/Will Not box: what does it control, and what if neither is checked?
cards.back: Whether the seller still owes the firm when another firm earns a commission under a new exclusive signed during holdover. Neither checked = not owed.

cards.front: Is holdover compensation owed on a sale to a Submitted Prospect with no new listing involved?
cards.back: Yes, if the sale happens within the holdover period stated in the listing.

cards.front: Disclosing offers when neither consent box is checked (listing contract)
cards.back: No consent. Disclosing terms always needs the seller's written consent.

cards.front: Present offers while under contract?
cards.back: Yes. All offers, in a timely manner (C.R.S. 12-10-404).

cards.front: Exclusive Right-to-Buy: neither relationship box checked
cards.back: The broker is a transaction-broker.

cards.front: Square Footage Disclosure: who completes it, and for what purpose
cards.back: The listing licensee. Marketing only. The buyer should measure independently if size matters.

cards.front: Source of Water Addendum choices
cards.back: Well (permit number), water provider, or other source described.

cards.front: Short Sale Acceptance Deadline missed
cards.back: The contract terminates.

cards.front: CFPA homeowner cancellation right
cards.back: Earlier of midnight of the 3rd business day after signing or noon on the day before the foreclosure sale.

cards.front: Who signs the Closing Instructions?
cards.back: Buyer, seller and the closing company.

cards.front: Deeds the closing company may prepare under the Closing Instructions
cards.back: Statutory deeds: general warranty, special warranty, bargain and sale, quitclaim.

cards.front: Three Commission deed of trust versions
cards.back: Due on Transfer–Strict, Due on Transfer–Creditworthy, Assumable–Not Due on Transfer.

cards.front: Trustee named in a Colorado deed of trust
cards.back: The county Public Trustee.

glossary.definition: A contract or form promulgated by the Colorado Real Estate Commission. Brokers must use one whenever one exists and is appropriate for the transaction.
The 1957 Colorado Supreme Court decision allowing brokers to fill in standard forms in transactions they handle, with no charge beyond their commission, even though doing so is the practice of law.
aliases: Conway-Bogue Realty v. Denver Bar Association

glossary.definition: The section of a Commission form where negotiated, transaction-specific terms are written. This language is not Commission-approved and must not amount to the broker practicing law.
The table near the front of a Colorado contract that lists every deadline (title, inspection, loan, appraisal, closing, possession) as a date or a number of days after MEC.
Mutual execution of contract: the date both parties have signed the contract. Many deadlines are counted from it.

An optional time in the Dates and Deadlines table that sets the cutoff for objection, resolution, examination and termination deadlines. If blank or N/A, those deadlines end at 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time.
A contract clause making deadlines strict. A late performance or notice is a breach or is ineffective.
A deposit from the buyer showing good faith. It is held in trust and applied at closing, returned, or forfeited under the contract.
The brokerage firm or closing company named in the contract to hold the earnest money in trust for both parties.
A negotiated later date for delivering earnest money, instead of delivering it with the contract.
The Commission form, signed by buyer and seller, that directs how earnest money is paid out and mutually releases the parties.
The deadline by which the buyer may terminate if the lender's underwriting is unsatisfactory. Missing it can make the earnest money nonrefundable.
Title as shown in the public records and the title commitment, including recorded liens, easements and covenants.
Matters affecting title that don't appear in the public records, such as unrecorded easements, boundary disputes or parties in possession.
Optional title coverage that removes the standard exceptions for unrecorded matters such as parties in possession, survey issues and unrecorded mechanics' liens.
A drawing by a surveyor showing where improvements sit relative to the boundaries. It is less precise than a full survey.
The owners' association's governing documents, insurance list, assessments, financial records and construction-defect notices that the seller provides to the buyer.
A statement from the owners' association showing the owner's account status and fees, requested by the seller before closing.
The Commission form a seller completes from current actual knowledge about the property's condition. It is not a warranty.
The buyer's written notice listing unsatisfactory conditions and the corrections requested, delivered by the Inspection Objection Deadline.
The Commission form, signed by buyer and seller, in which the seller agrees to specific corrections. It amends the contract.
An amount agreed in advance as the remedy for breach. In the Colorado contract, it is the earnest money kept by the seller as the seller's only remedy unless specific performance is selected.
A court order requiring a party to carry out the contract, for example to convey the property.
A nonbinding process in which a neutral third party helps the parties settle. Colorado contracts require it before arbitration or litigation.
The written notice a party delivers to end the contract under a specific provision. It is effective when the other party receives it by the deadline.
The Commission form used to respond to an offer with changed terms. It supersedes earlier counterproposals and expires without timely notice of acceptance.
The Commission form, signed by both parties, used to change deadlines or other terms of a signed contract.

A period after a listing or buyer agreement expires during which the firm can still earn compensation on a sale to a prospect (or property) submitted in writing during the term. A checkbox decides what happens if another firm earns a commission under a new exclusive signed during holdover.
Under the listing contract, a person the broker negotiated with whose name was given to the seller in writing during the listing period.
The Commission form, completed by the listing licensee, stating how square footage was measured or sourced. It is for marketing only.
The Commission addendum in which the seller identifies the property's water source: a well (with permit number), a water provider, or another source.
The federally required disclosure for housing built before 1978, including known hazards, the EPA pamphlet and the buyer's inspection opportunity.

Under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act, a buyer of a residence in foreclosure who won't occupy it as a principal residence. These sales carry special contract protections and cancellation rights.
The Commission form signed by buyer, seller and closing company that engages the closing company to prepare documents, close and disburse funds.
The borrower's written promise to repay a debt on stated terms. In seller financing, it is secured by a deed of trust.
The security instrument used in Colorado. The borrower conveys title to the county Public Trustee as security for the lender's note.
The county official who serves as trustee under Colorado deeds of trust and conducts foreclosures and releases.
